1: Open by asking who has lost a placement to a counteroffer. Most hands go up. The point of this session: almost every counteroffer can be seen coming, and the work to stop it happens at the first call, not at resignation.
2: Ask two people to share the deal they lost to a counteroffer. Write on the board when the warning signs first appeared. Usually it was early, and nobody asked the question.
3: Counteroffers usually happen when the candidate tells their employer they’re leaving, but the risk runs all the way from accepting the offer to their first day. Notice periods in the US are often two weeks, which is short, but contract and senior roles can be longer. Make the point: the stage before the danger window is where you do the work to defuse it.
4: Most counteroffers are a reaction to cost and disruption, not a sudden change of heart about the person. If the candidate is leaving for growth and the employer counters with money, the push factor hasn’t been fixed. Have the room take a live candidate and predict what their employer would offer, then match each item to the reason the candidate gave for leaving.
5: Handling counteroffers starts before any offer reaches the candidate. If you know the risk early, you can work on it with the client, for example by sharpening the offer on the thing the candidate cares about most. If the answer to the first question is “a raise would keep me”, that’s critical intel: either the motivation isn’t strong enough, or you need to build the case around the other push factors now. Pairs practise both questions, five minutes.
6: Present these as things to help the candidate think through, not threats. Avoid quoting statistics on how many counteroffer acceptors leave within a year unless you have a source you can show; candidates will push back on numbers that sound made up. The strongest argument is always their own push factors: “You told me you were leaving because of X. Does this offer change X?”
7: Counteroffers usually come with emotion, from a manager the candidate likes and respects. Never attack the employer. Acknowledge the sincerity, then bring the candidate back to their own reasons. Use silence after each question. The goal is a decision the candidate owns; if they genuinely choose to stay after thinking it through, respect it, keep the relationship and tell the client straight away.
8: This slide is new to the playbook. Resignation is the single highest-risk moment, so don’t leave it to chance. Help the candidate plan what they’ll say: grateful, brief, decided. Encourage a written resignation they can hand over. If a counteroffer comes up in the meeting, they thank their manager and say they’ve made their decision. Then they call you the same day. Keep weekly contact through the notice period.
9: The original playbook noted that if you know the risk early, your client may be able to influence it. Make that practical: a client who knows the candidate is leaving for progression can lead the offer with the title and growth path, not just salary. During notice, regular contact from the new manager is one of the most effective counteroffer defences. If a counter does land, bad news travels fast, so the client hears it from you first, with a plan.
10: Prepare scenario cards in advance. Example: candidate leaving for career growth, counter is a 10% raise and a vague promise of promotion. Another: candidate leaving for flexibility, counter is a new title. The trainee should never criticise the employer. Score them on: acknowledging the relationship, returning to push factors, asking the “why now?” question, and letting the candidate decide.
11: Go back to the deals lost to counteroffers from the start of the session. Which slide would have saved each one? Ask everyone to name the candidate they’ll ask the counteroffer question this week.
12: Open the floor for questions. This is the last core module: point people back to the master Training Programme for the 12-week schedule and the live-desk sign-off.
